blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights that Linux's core operations have seen performance degradation or significant fluctuations over the past seven years, contrary to expectations. The paper reveals that 75% of kernel operations are slower than seven years ago, with notable slowdowns after version 4.8. The author emphasizes the substantial effort required to tune the Linux kernel, noting that large enterprises like Google employ over 100 engineers for 6-18 months per kernel release to optimize performance. The paper identifies 11 root causes for performance issues, categorized into security enhancements (e.g., Meltdown/Spectre mitigations), new features, and configuration changes. Disabling these root causes can yield significant performance improvements (up to 56% for Redis), though this may not be practical for most users. The analysis underscores the trade-off between security, new features, and performance, as well as the complexity of kernel configuration.
paper_title: An analysis of performance evolution of Linux’s core operations
